statement: A figure carries only symbols and data: a schematic (circuit, block diagram) uses symbols, signal names and component labels only, and no explanatory note, annotation or text box sits inside any figure; explanatory text goes in the caption.
why: A schematic shows structure, not a case.
provenance: writing-style rule 20; user ruling 2026-11-09; self-check; merged figure.no-notes-in-figure, caption.holds-notes (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G5)

statement: Text, figures and captions agree: every term, symbol, label and claim in a figure, axis label, legend and caption matches the text; a figure never keeps a label the text has dropped. How a needed figure change is applied follows the write skill's hard constraints (proposal first, applied only after approval).
why: A stale label contradicts the text.

statement: Panels of one figure share a baseline and a common height, one font size and one colour scheme, with legible ticks and legends at print size; inspect the compiled page before finishing.
why: Mismatched panels look like two figures.

statement: Never place a single half-width panel alone on a row when a related panel can share it; pair related panels or widen the plot.
why: Empty half rows waste the page budget.

statement: Each y-axis ends just above its tallest data, with the headroom of dimension figure.y-headroom; no empty band.
why: An empty band wastes space and misleads.

statement: Colour never carries a distinction alone: double every colour difference with a line style, marker or hatch, so the figure survives greyscale and colour-vision deficiency; avoid red against green. Use the palette of dimension figure.palette, defined once and reused by every figure.
why: Many readers print in grey or see colours differently.

statement: One quantity keeps one colour and one style across all figures, including schematics.
why: The reader learns the code once.

statement: Label curves directly where space allows; a legend is the fallback.
why: Direct labels save the eye a trip.

statement: Every unusual feature of a plotted curve (kink, peak, outlier) is explained in the text or caption; describe the relationship behind a trend, not only its direction.
why: An unexplained feature is a question left open.

statement: All figure text is drawn at its printed size in the size of dimension figure.font-size-pt; include the figure unscaled when dimension figure.scaling says unscaled.
why: Scaled figures change their text size.
provenance: user ruling 2026-11-12 (figure text 8 pt); P18 (text size part)

statement: No text element overlaps another; verify numerically, not by eye.

A text or label change never alters panel widths, gaps, figure size or margins. Fit the text inside the existing layout; if it cannot fit, report it with options before touching the layout. Compare the layout with the saved baseline after every change.
why: Layout drift breaks an approved figure.
good: one-line x label after the panel letter (label_after_letter)
bad: widening a panel to fit a label

statement: Place figures and tables near the discussion that cites them, not at the end of the document.
why: The reader sees the evidence where the argument uses it.
